reason: The text presents Moses and Aaron as advocates for the Hebrew people, not antagonists. They are sent by God to demand Pharaoh's release of the Israelites from slavery. While the initial escalation of hardship (removal of straw while maintaining brick quotas) triggers complaints from the Hebrew overseers, this reflects the unintended consequence of resistance to oppression, not antagonism toward their own people. Moses explicitly expresses concern for the people's suffering (וַיָּשָׁב מֹשֶׁה אֶל־ יְהוָה... 'Why have you brought evil upon this people?'). Both leaders intercede through prayer on behalf of the people during the plagues, and the text shows them persistently working toward the people's liberation. The Hebrew people's frustration with their leaders stems from the worsening of immediate conditions during the liberation process, not from any hostility by the leaders toward their own people.
